speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Among risk factors, tobacco use is the second highest contributor to ill-health and premature death in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Singapore's long-standing public health objective is to promote and move towards a tobacco-free society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: To this end, over the years, Singapore has adopted a comprehensive, multi-pronged approach to tobacco control with the aim of, among others: (a) preventing or reducing the opportunities for non-smokers, particularly youths, to pick up smoking; (b) encouraging existing smokers to quit; and (c) encouraging Singaporeans to adopt a tobacco-free lifestyle.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Over the years, measures adopted as part of our multi-pronged approach have included banning smoking in certain public places, restricting tobacco advertising and promotion, introducing mandatory graphic health warnings (GHWs) on tobacco product packaging, banning the use of misleading descriptors, such as "mild" and "light", on tobacco products and also imposing taxes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: However, in recent years, the decline in smoking rates has been harder to sustain.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The smoking rates have been fluctuating between 12% and 14% in the last 10 years, with no clear pattern of continuous decline.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: More than one in five men smoke daily, and our male smoking rate is higher than that in Australia, New Zealand, the UK and the US.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Clearly, we need to do more to stem tobacco use among Singaporeans, with a view to denormalising the use of tobacco products and bringing overall smoking rates to a level that is as low as possible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: To this end, over the last few years, we have been studying best practices in other countries, as well as the recommendations adopted under the auspices of the World Health Organization (WHO) with respect to the implementation of the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (FCTC), which Singapore is a party to.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We have consulted extensively on new tobacco control measures, which include banning displays of tobacco products at the retail point-of-sale, increasing the size of graphic health warnings, raising the minimum age for tobacco, and a prohibition on flavoured tobacco products.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The ban on point-of-sale tobacco product displays took effect in August 2017, with the aim of reducing exposure of non-smokers, especially youths, to the advertising effect of such displays, and discouraging impulse purchases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Slightly over a year ago, this Parliament also passed legislative changes to increase the Minimum Legal Age for the purchase, use, possession, sale and supply of tobacco products.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Excise duty on tobacco products was raised by 10% last year to further discourage Singaporeans' consumption of tobacco products.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We are now continuing with our multi-pronged approach to tobacco control by introducing a measure that the FCTC Guidelines call on parties to consider adopting and, that is, the standardised packaging of tobacco products.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The design of tobacco products and packaging is used to promote tobacco products among adults and the young alike.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Key elements of tobacco packaging include brand imagery, logos, colours and, of course, the pack design.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Cigarette packs serve as a "five-second commercial" whenever the pack is drawn from the shelf or one's pocket, held in the palm of a hand, or placed in full view on the table.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Independent research and reviews of tobacco industry documents have found that packaging is an effective marketing medium that helps to build direct relationships between the tobacco company and the consumer through possession and use.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Packaging innovation, design and value packaging are used not only to distinguish products from competitors but also to promote the product, communicate brand values and target specific consumer groups.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Evidence suggests that the appeal of branded packaging also acts as one of the factors encouraging children and young adults to experiment with tobacco and to establish and thereafter continue the habit of smoking.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Standardised packaging of tobacco products generally refers to: (a) the strict regulation of promotional aspects of tobacco packaging; and (b) standardisation of packaging elements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This includes removing all logos, colours, brand images and promotional information on packaging, other than brand names and product names, which include the variants, displayed in a standard colour and font style.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: It is often accompanied by a third element, namely, the incorporation of prominent mandatory health warnings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Singapore is not the first country to consider introducing standardised packaging of tobacco products.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This amounted to about 25% of the 2.2 percentage point decline in smoking prevalence during that period.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: In 2018, a study conducted by the French Department of Public Health found that one million daily smokers in the country quit the habit between 2016 and 2017.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This decline, which was described by the French authorities as "historic", was attributed to a raft of tobacco control measures implemented in 2016, including standardised packaging.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Other countries have also moved towards standardised packaging.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The UK, Ireland, New Zealand and Norway have fully implemented standardised packaging measures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Thailand, Hungary, Saudi Arabia, Slovenia and Uruguay are at varying stages of implementing standardised packaging, while Canada recently concluded a public consultation on the draft specifications on the proposed measure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Burkina Faso, Georgia and Romania have passed enabling legislation for standardised packaging but have yet to announce the date for full implementation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Other countries considering standardised packaging at the legislative or governmental level include Brazil, Chile, Ecuador, Panama, South Africa, Sri Lanka and Mauritius.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: A local study carried out by the Health Promotion Board (HPB) to assess Singaporeans' perceptions of current and plainer cigarette product packaging found that the current cigarette pack designs influence both smokers' and non-smokers' perceptions towards various attributes of the cigarette packs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Attractive pack designs were associated with high-quality cigarettes and increased likelihood of attracting youths to try such products.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Amongst a significant minority of non-smokers, the perceived pack attractiveness was associated with the intention to try smoking.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: In contrast, plainer or standardised packs were generally seen as less attractive, compared to current cigarette packs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: HPB's findings from other local studies also indicated that packs with darker colours and at least 75% graphic warnings were considered by Singaporeans to be least attractive and perceived to be more harmful to health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Health warnings on packs with at least 75% graphic warnings and darker colours were also more noticeable, compared to packs with just 50% graphic warnings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Between 2010 and 2018, the Ministry of Health (MOH) engaged in a continuous process of reviewing and evaluating a substantial body of international research related to tobacco product marketing and standardised packaging.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The Ministry has also received a range of feedback, comments and concerns with respect to the possible introduction of standardised packaging over the years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: All of these have been carefully considered and addressed in detail in two papers published by my Ministry in support of and in response to the public consultations carried out in 2018.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: These public health objectives, in turn, both taken separately, individually and together, and in conjunction with other existing tobacco control measures, are expected to contribute to achieving Singapore's broader tobacco control aims, which include discouraging non-smokers from even picking up smoking, encouraging smokers to quit, and encouraging Singaporeans to adopt a tobacco-free lifestyle.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Under the new section 17, all tobacco products, and the packaging or labelling of tobacco products, must comply with every requirement prescribed in subsidiary legislation, including requirements as to size, appearance, design, health warnings and other information to be stated.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Also, tobacco products and their packaging or labelling must not bear any trade mark, term, descriptor, figurative or other sign, feature, scent or sound that is prescribed as prohibited, or promotes the tobacco product by any means that is false, misleading, deceptive or likely to create an erroneous impression about its characteristics, health effects, hazards or emissions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The latter is in line with the prohibition under the current section 17A of the Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The import into Singapore, and the distribution, sale, offer for sale or possession for sale in Singapore, of such non-compliant tobacco products will be made an offence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: In addition, clause 6 of the Bill amends section 37 to empower the Minister for Health to make Regulations with respect to the size, appearance and design of tobacco products and their packaging and labelling, the health warnings and also other information displayed on such products, including the trademarks, terms, descriptors, features, scents and sounds that I mentioned will be prohibited in relation to tobacco products and their packaging and labelling.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: As the papers published by my Ministry in support of and in response to the public consultations conducted in 2018 have stated, our proposal for Singapore's standardised packaging measures will comprise of two parts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: All permitted information, such as brand names and product names, would be required to be displayed in a standard colour and a standard font style.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The colour, size, shape, opening and finish of the retail packaging will also be standardised, as will aspects of the appearance of the tobacco product.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Following the passage of this Bill – should this Bill be passed – subsidiary legislation will be made to implement the SP proposal, which will then replace the current Tobacco (Control of Advertisements and Sale) (Labelling) Regulations 2012.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: One of the key features of the SP Proposal is the prohibition on the use of any branding and that includes the logos, colours and other features associated with the tobacco brand, advertising and promotional elements, from being displayed on tobacco product packaging or the products themselves.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This is the case except for brand names and product names that will be required to be displayed in a standard font and colour, as I mentioned.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: There have been concerns expressed that this prohibition would unduly impinge on the industry's intellectual property (IP) rights and would not be consistent with international IP law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The Government maintains its strong commitment to the protection of IP rights.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: It is also our view that the SP Proposal is consistent with Singapore's international obligations in relation to IP rights.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Tobacco companies' trademarks do not give them absolute rights to use their trademarks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Those rights are subject to legitimate Government regulation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The measures proposed in Australia were not dissimilar to what is being proposed in this Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Nonetheless, as a further assurance to rights-holders that the SP Proposal will not affect their ability to otherwise maintain and enforce their IP rights, clause 7 of the Bill introduces new provisions which will make it clear that the implementation of standardised packaging in Singapore will not affect the registrability and registration of tobacco-related trademarks and designs under the Trade Marks Act and the Registered Designs Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Clause 2 of the Bill inserts a new definition of "trademark" to clarify that the term has the same meaning as that in the Trade Marks Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: As mentioned, clause 6 confers on the Minister the power to make subsidiary legislation setting out the details of the packaging measures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The key specifications were set out in the public consultation paper on the SP Proposal, which was published in February last year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: In particular, it was made clear that the proposed measures would include standardising both the internal and the external surfaces of all retail packages, standardising the shape and dimensions of the retail package, and standardising the branding and product information allowed on retail packaging, including location, typeface, colours and size.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We recognise and acknowledge that the introduction of standardised packaging will have an impact on tobacco and other related industries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Nevertheless, the positive objectives as well as the public health outcomes that the SP Proposal is expected to achieve warrants its introduction.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Should this Bill be passed, to facilitate smooth implementation of the new measures, we will be meeting with manufacturers, importers, distributors and retailers of cigarettes, cigars and other tobacco products retailed in Singapore to brief them on the proposed specifications for the standardised layouts for tobacco product packaging and other operational issues.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Sufficient notice will also be given to the industry of the finalised specifications, and prior to the new requirements taking effect, manufacturers and retailers will be permitted to start producing and selling standardised packs alongside existing packs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This "sell through" period will allow retailers to clear their existing stocks of branded tobacco products and ease the implementation burden.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Next, I will touch on several other amendments in the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The latter amount is increased from the current $2,000, which has been an amount which has not been raised since the Act was first enacted more than 25 years ago.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This proposed increase aims to regain parity with similar provisions in other legislation and to ensure that the deterrent remains effective.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This aligns the penalties under section 18 with the maximum fines for similarly serious offences pertaining to the importation, distribution, retail and possession of prohibited tobacco products and imitation tobacco products under sections 15 and 16 of the Act, respectively.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The Government is committed to reducing the serious harm that tobacco products cause to individual Singaporeans and to the nation's public health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Our long-standing public health objective is to promote and move towards a tobacco-free society and it is to this end that we have consistently adopted a multi-pronged approach to tobacco control.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We further recognise that continuing efforts in tobacco control are necessary to sustain the declines in smoking rates and also bring the overall smoking rate to a level that is as low as possible.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I believe that plain or standard packaging will prove to be another nail in the coffin for smoking, a habit which has brought grief and misery through ill-health to generations of smokers and their loved ones.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The post-implementation data from Australia, which was the first country to introduce standard packaging for tobacco products in 2012, and also from France, reinforces the efficacy of such a measure.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Tobacco companies and the lobby groups associated with them have decried that plain packaging would have little effect on smoking rates except to make life more vexatious for retailers and their customers, but their robust efforts to fight against standard packaging, for example, by launching lawsuits against Australia, proves that this is otherwise.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The tobacco industry is running scared, thus underlining the potential impact of standard packaging legislation on smoking rates.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With the passing of this amendment, Singapore will join several countries besides Australia which have already enacted this legislation, and many other countries are expected to follow.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Standard packaging is a measure that is endorsed by WHO which, in 2016, on World No Tobacco Day, exhorted all countries to prepare to introduce plain packaging for tobacco products.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There are two concerns that have been raised about plain packaging or standard packaging that I would like to ask the Minister to address so as to reassure the House that these potential consequences will not come to bear.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This could conversely lead to cheaper products increasing market share and may, in theory, lead to increased smoking due to cheaper products and more affordable products coming to the forefront.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Is there any evidence for this concern, and what are the measures to ensure that plain packaging does not play into the hands of counterfeiters?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I look forward to the Ministry's responses on these points, and I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Other countries are in the process of doing so.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am glad that Singapore is not far behind in this.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: According to studies done, the idea of plain packaging is to prevent or reduce any positive association of branding with the consumption of tobacco.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It seems that such positive association of branding will attract young people who are new to smoking, even giving such false sense of glamour associated with certain brands.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: According to the studies, requiring the use of standard unattractive colours, reducing font sizes for brand name, highlighting or magnifying health warnings, are effective in deterring new smokers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MOH's requirement of health warning by way of graphic images will definitely contribute to the deglamourising of smoking for the young.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: According to reports from Australia, the use of plain packaging seemed to have reduced smoking among young people, as people found that their packaging was not attractive.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some even had the impression cigarettes in plain packaging had tasted worse.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many people picked up smoking when they were young, including, in the case of Singapore, during National Service.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Together with the recent increase in the legal age for smoking to eventually 21, I hope that the introduction of plain packaging will, like in Australia or elsewhere, help to discourage more young people from picking up smoking.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the other hand, we also read of attempts of tobacco companies in other countries to work around the limitations of plain packaging by, for example, introducing features to maintain product appeal, even when sold in plain packaging, such as resealable inner foil to preserve freshness and innovative filters.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some had tried to have unique packaging which do not appear to meet the minimum size required for health information on the side of packs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It seems that these design tweaks are important for some of these tobacco companies as they appeal to young adults and may lead to increased sales.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I also read that in some countries, tobacco companies were given a relatively long time to get rid of their existing stocks and to transit to plain packaging and that some companies also deliberately stalled on the introduction of plain packaging or were not cooperative.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does the Government intend to introduce changes to the law to deal with any such inconsistency?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does the Government have any plans to standardise the size of cigarettes being sold?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.30 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.10 pm until 3.30 pm.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: From expanding no-smoking zones to regulating displays of tobacco sales to increasing the minimum legal age for buying cigarettes and more, the Government has shown its commitment to the tobacco-free movement.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In November last year, the Government revealed plans to standardise the packaging of tobacco.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This follows in the footsteps of countries like Australia, France, the UK and many others which have adopted similar standardised packaging policies.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: With today’s Bill, we will be a major step closer to this goal.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The last press release from MOH stated that a transition period will be provided to allow manufacturers and retailers to sell their old stock.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am concerned about the vendors who sell cigarettes in the small provision shops and mama shops in the heartlands and the bus stops.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many of the shop keepers are elderly, and they are already facing many challenges to keep their business afloat.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Has the Ministry reached out to them to help them understand the new regulations and to check if they would have trouble meeting the established deadlines?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In the meantime, I would like to take the opportunity to urge the Government to consider adding designated smoking points (DSPs) to more places, especially in the heartlands.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In the last update on this issue in February 2018, the Senior Minister of State said she would look into the results of the study of Orchard Road to see how this project can be expanded.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, Orchard Road and the heartlands are rather different in demographic and environment, amongst many other things.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We can shield the vulnerable from second-hand smoke.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Children will also not be over-exposed to the sight of people smoking, preventing the normalising of smoking in their minds.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, smokers’ needs are met, too.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The reality is that some smokers simply will not quit.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They have told me that they appreciate the DSPs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It helps them reduce the times they smoke at home, which exposes their family to second-hand smoke, or can lead to disputes with neighbours.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, from time to time, I do receive requests and emails from residents from other parts of Singapore asking for DSPs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, I hope the Government will seriously look into having more DSPs in residential areas.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Furthermore, I hope the Government will allow the Community Improvement Projects Committee fund to be used for the construction and maintenance of DSPs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I believe DSPs will certainly be win-win for both smokers and non-smokers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I wish to share my concerns about the increasing popularity of contraband cigarettes.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is inevitable as regulations concerning tobacco get tighter and cigarettes become more expensive.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In the past months, the Singapore Police Force has conducted raids turning up large numbers of contraband cigarettes.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Industrial areas and foreign-worker dormitories were among the places targeted.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that Singapore Customs also conducts island-wide enforcement operations.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But what if the couriers working for the syndicates are being assured that their fines would be paid for if caught?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Why do we not add in a jail term?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: A news report in 2017 revealed that illegal syndicates hire foreign workers to deliver the contraband cigarettes.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Has there been an improvement in the situation since?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Exposure to cigarettes and smoking among foreign workers are also an issue we should be concerned about.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that the Ministry is working with dormitory operators and contractor companies to reach out to these workers to advise them about the laws concerning smoking in Singapore, and the unhealthy effects of smoking and second-hand smoke.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: These workers come to Singapore to seek a better living for themselves and their families, and it would be a shame for them to squander the money away on vices and picking up poor health that could have a negative impact on their health in the long run.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, some of these foreign workers are living in our Housing and Development Board units and smoke along the corridor.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Just last week, I had a house visit, and a mother shared with me her agony.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: She has three young children, and the unit beside hers is rented out to several foreign workers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: She said that almost every night, they smoke along the corridor, and the smoke drifts into her unit.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: She was so afraid that the second-hand smoke would have ill-effects on the health of her three young children.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: As a mother, I can fully understand her desire to protect her children.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, in this case, I alerted the National Environment Agency (NEA) and asked them to step up enforcement action because smoking along the corridor is not permitted under the current law.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: On this note, I would like to once again bring up the increasing complaints of neighbours smoking in their own units and the smoke drifting into the neighbours' units and affecting the neighbours.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Is NEA determined to do something about it?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Or is the MOH determined to do something about it?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I know that smoking is a personal choice, just like you can have parties in your own home so long as the noise generated does not affect the neighbours.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, you can smoke in your own home, but the smoke should not affect your neighbours.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Of course, we hope that the neighbours can be more considerate and think of the neighbours before they light up the cigarette.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They can perhaps make use of the DSPs or walk further away.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But I really hope that MOH can work with NEA to come out together to address this issue.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   	I am glad that the Government is continuously introducing new measures to reduce the smoking rate.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is a good idea to ban eye-catching cigarette packaging.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In Yishun South, the feedback on our DSPs is very positive.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the Government will allow the Community Improvement Project Committee Fund to be used for the construction and maintenance of the DSPs.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: This proposed move towards clean packaging will align Singapore with WHO's Framework Convention on Tobacco Control along with countries, such as Australia, France, New Zealand and the UK, which have also mandated standardised packaging for tobacco products.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Such a concerted effort to stamp out smoking is crucial because it exacts a significant toll on our society, as the Senior Minister of State noted earlier.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: According to a study published in Asia and the Pacific Policy Studies, smoking prevalence in Singapore approximates 15% among adults and 6% among youths aged 13 to 15.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, studies in other parts of the world have shown that people who smoke during adolescence are 16 times more likely to become adult smokers.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Given the evidence that early experimentation with smoking is a predictor for smoking dependency in adulthood, we must, therefore, do our utmost to discourage our young from acquiring this harmful habit.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: This is the circumvention of restrictions on tobacco advertising by multinational tobacco companies through the use of insidious social media campaigns.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: These campaigns capitalise on the appeal of social media influencers through photographs featuring these young role models smoking in cool venues while wearing trendy clothing, accompanied by catchy hashtags.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Deceptively, however, no explicit mention is made of the tobacco companies behind these campaigns.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Such visually arresting content seeks to depict smoking as a normal practice among young people and, indeed, showcases smoking as a glamorous and desirable lifestyle choice.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: In the US, the Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids has led several organisations, including the American Academy of Paediatrics and the American Lung Association, to mount a petition requesting action by the US Federal Trade Commission.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: This petition asserts that tobacco companies are actively promoting smoking via hundreds of thousands of images, hashtags and videos shared by young people on social media platforms, such as Instagram, Facebook and Twitter.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: These multinational tobacco companies have initiated such media campaigns in numerous countries throughout Asia, Europe, the Middle East and Central, North and South America, roping in high-profile youth influencers in each country.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Closer to home, tobacco companies have funded such campaigns in neighbouring countries, such as Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Thailand.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Influencers are given strict instructions on which cigarettes to feature, how to take natural photographs which do not resemble advertisements, when they should post these images for optimal audience engagement, as well as the hashtags that they must use.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: In one particular country, the influencers were even told to conceal the health warnings on the cigarette packs before posting the images.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Such shady tactics are calculated to mislead young people into thinking that these images are organic social media content that simply reflect youth culture.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: While there is fortunately no evidence to show that social media influencers in Singapore have been targeted by tobacco companies in this way, the porous and borderless nature of the Internet means that young Singaporeans can nevertheless be exposed to such images.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Many social media influencers also have a global fan base, so even campaigns originating from well beyond our shores can appeal to our youths if influencers with a strong following in Singapore are mobilised.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: After all, Singaporeans are avid social media users, with young Singaporeans being the most active.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Of particular pertinence to Singapore is the fact that most of these social media campaigns promoting smoking almost exclusively use English even when it is not the lingua franca of the country from which these campaigns originate.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The highly visual nature of social media platforms, such as Instagram, Facebook and Snapchat, also means that language is essentially no barrier to the communicative impact of such images.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: This is yet another issue, in addition to online falsehoods, that shows how the extensive reach of big technology companies with a global presence has significant ramifications on society.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Because of the lack of transparency surrounding the algorithms that determine what content social media platforms serve us, we cannot discern why we may be seeing more of particular forms of content.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Neither can we exert more active control over our social media feeds should we so choose.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Young people who like, share or comment on images portraying negative behaviours as hip and trendy, with particular hashtags, may be unwittingly served more of such images on their social media feeds.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: These companies possess the ability to alter their algorithms to stem the spread of such images, in the same way that they have algorithms to weed out obscene and extremist content.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   	Although this Bill will help promote plain tobacco packaging, for the young, curbing smoking at the sales stage may already be too late.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The young can be easily influenced by the positive image of smoking created by social media marketing.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Such marketing is sponsored by multinational tobacco companies.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Although there are no such marketing campaigns in Singapore thus far, the borderless nature of the Internet means that our young can come into contact with these positive images of smoking through social media, such as Instagram and Snapchat.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, social media has become a new area where our health authorities must battle the marketing strategy of depicting smoking as a desirable lifestyle choice.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: MOH must work with other countries and WHO to take action to fight this unhealthy trend.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: (In Malay):   	Mr Speaker, it is hoped that standardised packaging for cigarettes will, firstly, make it less attractive to smokers, especially the younger generation and those who want to try smoking and have just started smoking; second, reduce the impact of advertisements and promotions; third, further strengthen messages about the negative impact and dangers of smoking; fourth, create clearer graphics on the risks and warnings about smoking on its packaging.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: These measures will, hopefully, further reduce the number of smokers and also stop those who intend to start smoking.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It is also in line with the WHO Convention to further reduce the number of smokers globally.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: But will these measures have an impact, especially on our Malay community?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: They have the highest number of smokers at the national level.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: What can we do to manage this situation?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Health statistics show that the number of our community members who are unhealthy, in terms of having chronic diseases and a smoking habit as one of the risks, are worrying.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Our Malay male smokers, for instance, start smoking at a young age, during their teens and even while in school.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Parents who smoke introduce the risk of second-hand smoke to their children and family members, and this will further increase their risk.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We must unite in our efforts to address this problem together.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It is hoped that these messages, and the age limit to buy cigarettes, as well as negative psychological messages, will have an impact on this complex smoking problem.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: (In English): Is standardised packaging going to work for Singapore?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: So, are we still going ahead with it?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In considering this, it brings us to the root cause of, firstly, the association between cigarette smoking and cigarette pack designs, the pack attributes and also people’s choices.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Thirdly, the potential impact of the graphic warnings and advisories.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: And there have been studies that have been quoted, both pro and also against this.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: As regulators, they must also ask themselves in planning programmes and enforcements, which include the link between package and design with quality, taste, cost, social appeal, attempt to start and try smoking, and also the ease of quitting and perhaps the perceived harm – amongst the different age groups and different generations.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The issue and the problem lie in the fact that these factors affect people differently and unpredictably as well.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It is coloured by their upbringing, life experiences, perceptions, inculcation of educational messages into their neural networks and also their psychological resilience and makeup.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Those are, indeed, complex elements for us to really control.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: After knowing all these factors, are we going ahead with this Bill?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Because we owe it to those who will be impacted, to those who will benefit, to those who will quit, to those who will not start and to those who are affected by other people smoking around them.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Therefore, it may be short-sighted to actually just view this Bill as a single entity.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It is something that should be seen in the bigger context of Singapore as a clean and green garden city, in the context of making the presence of smoking restriction framework in our public places common with the fact that we have age restriction limits to purchasing of cigarette and tobacco products and, of course, our ongoing educational efforts and I QUIT programmes that have been implemented over years and generations.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: All these are also important because we want to make sure that our younger generations stay healthy for years to come.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In fact, one of the programmes that is targeting the younger generations will be the smoke-free tobacco generation, that is, for those who are born in the year 2000 and beyond to actually stop smoking.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: And I think we have been quite active with this programme in our schools and with teenagers as well.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: So, therefore, when we consider all these put together, hopefully, it will be more positive than negative.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Studies from other countries that have implemented standardised packaging, such as those in Australia and the UK, consistently highlight the deterrent effect this measure can have upon smoking.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The implementation of standardised packaging is a huge and positive leap in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That being said, I would like to seek some clarifications on certain aspects of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, I would like to seek clarification on the increase in the maximum fines that may be imposed for offences relating to licences required for dealing with tobacco products.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Could the Minister for Health clarify the rationale behind the increase in maximum fines for such offences?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Is there evidence, for instance, from studies conducted in other countries that such an increase in maximum fines would be effective in deterring offenders, especially in the case of repeat offenders?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Are there reasons as to why they have been increased by this specific amount?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Has there also been an increase in recent times for such offences?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, under the new section 17, the Bill requires that all tobacco products that are imported, distributed and sold in Singapore adhere to the requirements prescribed under the principal Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify exactly how these requirements would be enforced?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would the original powers of the Police and authorised officials be adequate, particularly given the introduction of a considerable measure, such as standardised packaging?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This committee monitors potential contraventions and decides what type of punitive actions should be taken based on the contraventions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Such a committee could be particularly useful in ensuring that the standardised packaging proposal is implemented smoothly in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Does the Ministry have any plans to set up a similar enforcement committee to ensure that there is a separate institutionalised body responsible for all matters concerning enforcement of standardised packaging?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: According to MOH's Press Release on 31 October last year, standardised packaging is intended to fulfill five main objectives.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These include reducing the packaging's potential to mislead consumers on the harmful effects of smoking, highlighting GHWs, and raising awareness about the risks of smoking.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, according to the primary study used in the Australian government’s review of its standardised packaging programme, researchers found that the measure did not adequately address the goal of reducing the ability of tobacco packaging to mislead smokers on the harmful effects of smoking.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, the study found that there was no change in smokers' misperceptions that certain types of tobacco products were better for their health.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Could the Minister clarify exactly how and why standardised packaging would reduce the potential of tobacco packaging to mislead consumers on the harmful effects of smoking then?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, the study also discussed the inclusion of colour names in brand variant names after the implementation of standardised plain packaging in Australia.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As standardised packaging in Australia did not limit the use of colour names in brand variant names, companies began including colour names to evoke the sensations or feelings previously connoted by the colour on the package.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, a product, which was known as "Dunhill Distinct" in the past, had its brand variant name changed to "Dunhill Distinct Blue" after the introduction of standardised packaging.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Such efforts had the effect of reinforcing the differences between tobacco products which further contributes to the misconception that certain product variants were less harmful than others.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given the potential ramifications which can result from certain brand variant names, could the Ministry consider vetting and setting restrictions on certain brand variant names?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, based on the example I have used, would it be possible to prohibit the use of colour names in brand variant names?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill signals the Government’s firm willingness to work towards creating a tobacco-free Singapore and I wholeheartedly support these efforts.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I share the Ministry's concern that after so many years of public education, the number of smokers in Singapore has not actually decreased as much as we hope for.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have to invest more effort into solving this addiction problem, especially among the younger smokers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Standardised packaging will remove the illusions of their purported attributes and enable shoppers to see them as they are – tobacco – nothing more and nothing less.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Since the producers were required to include graphic warnings on the cigarette packs sold, have the different health warnings been effective?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the Ministry consider requiring the producers to restrict the percentage of nicotine content and other harmful contents?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the Ministry consider requiring all media to carry reminders of the harmful effects of tobacco in all screenings of videos, movies or drama productions where the scenes of smoking cannot be edited and cut?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I will now address the Members' queries on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is a statistic we do not want to see and want to arrest and reverse.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Tobacco use, including smoking, remains, therefore, a significant public health problem in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Our long-standing public health objective is to promote and move towards a tobacco-free society, a point that several Members have reiterated earlier as well.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This Bill is another in the suite of tools we have introduced, and which we will continue to introduce as necessary, to control tobacco consumption.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Prof Fatimah Lateef has made the point that it would be short-sighted to view this Bill as a single entity.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The SP Proposal must, therefore, be seen in the context of Singapore’s various multi-pronged approaches to tobacco control.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Our approach includes a comprehensive mix of strategies, and that includes public education, the provision of smoking cessation services, taxation and legislation, amongst other things, to control tobacco labelling, advertising and promotion, smoking in public places and sales of cigarettes to minors, all of which work in tandem to control tobacco consumption.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng has asked for clarification on how standardised packaging can be expected to reduce the potential of tobacco packaging to mislead consumers on the harmful effects of smoking.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In particular, he suggests that certain studies found that Australia’s standardised packaging measures did not adequately address the goal of reducing the ability of tobacco packaging to mislead smokers on the harmful effects of smoking.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There is a broad and extensive range of international and local research and evidence which shows that standardised packaging is likely to be effective in meeting public health objectives – the five points which I have outlined earlier.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: MOH has also taken into consideration the feedback from our several public consultations in formulating our final assessment of the evidence pertaining to the SP Proposal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Studies internationally have found that through the elimination of logo and design elements, plain packs were perceived as less attractive, less attention-grabbing, and less likely to be purchased by youths, compared to branded and novel packs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Indeed, the US Surgeon-General’s Report in 2012 concluded that "there is strong, consistent evidence that advertising and promotion influence the factors that lead directly to tobacco use by adolescents, including the initiation of cigarette smoking as well as its continuation".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Therefore, addressing the labelling and packaging of tobacco products is an important step towards reducing smoking uptake and prevalence.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is also aligned to what WHO itself recommends under the FCTC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: WHO concluded in 2016 that, "there is a large body of empirical evidence… for introduction of standardised packaging", and that this evidence "suggests that standardised packaging makes health warnings, restrictions on tobacco advertising, promotion and sponsorship, as well as restrictions on misleading tobacco packaging more effective".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In April 2015, after the introduction of the measures in Australia, the Australian government published its Post-Implementation Review data in a series of peer-reviewed journal papers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The studies concluded that the objectives of Australia's plain packaging measure had been met and again, I quote, "plain packaging is severely restricting the ability of the pack to communicate and create appeal with young people and adults", and "plain packaging   fulfilling its core aims of reducing appeal, particularly among young adults, and increasing warning salience."  Indeed, studies in Australia after the introduction of plain packaging also found that there were behavioural outcomes associated with greater quit intention, and also negative feelings towards tobacco products.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For instance, in one study, the number of quit attempts rose after implementation of the measure.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There was also evidence that smokers avoided displaying the standardised packs and there was greater avoidance behaviour regarding GHWs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: While it is, of course, very challenging to seek to isolate the impact of any one single tobacco control policy, it is noteworthy that in the Australian experience, they have had access to a large, granular dataset collected over an extended period of time.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Analysis of this dataset indicates that over a period of 34 months, after accounting for other tobacco control measures, Australia's standardised packaging measure contributed to a 0.55 percentage point decline in smoking prevalence that was above and beyond existing trends.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Although 0.55% may seem small, nonetheless it is still impactful.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Together with our own experts, we reviewed this study in some detail.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have access to the dataset itself, so we did not just review their conclusions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We looked at their datasets in some detail, and we have found that its methodology and conclusions were thorough, reliable and credible.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: All of these are very useful indicators which tell us that the SP Proposal that we have put up is the correct measure to take.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Overall, the evidence supports the conclusion that the SP Proposal is likely, alongside other tobacco-control measures, to promote public health through the reduction of the prevalence of smoking in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Whilst there can be no precise prediction on future behavioural trends, or how long the impact might take to be felt, or whether other measures might become necessary to achieve even better tobacco control, the current evidence points substantially in favour of there being significant public health benefit in Singapore with the introduction of the SP Proposal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked about the effectiveness of health warnings.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The aim of GHWs on tobacco products is precisely to communicate health risks and also to motivate tobacco users and, possibly, potential users, to either quit or reduce, or not even start consumption.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This question has previously been addressed by MOH in this House.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Members will know that there is a strong body of international evidence demonstrating the impact of GHWs on knowledge of health effects, thoughts about quitting, use of Quitlines, and ultimately on quitting attempts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Studies from Australia, Canada, the US and the UK have shown impact on behaviours, such as noticing cigarette warnings and forgoing cigarettes, predict subsequent quitting attempts among individual smokers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Locally, in Singapore, a 2005 study by HPB evaluating the impact of the introduction of GHWs showed that 50% of participants were more concerned and worried about their health after seeing the GHWs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This also led to behaviour changes where one in four smokers were motivated to quit smoking and made efforts to abstain from smoking.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Non-smokers were also affected and more than half spoke up to advise their friends and loved ones to quit smoking.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This outcome and finding are also consistent with international evidence on the impact of GHWs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The evidence also suggests that the use of large and noticeable GHWs can reduce smoking initiation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: WHO recommends that countries should consider increasing the size of GHWs to cover more than 50% of tobacco packaging and replacing the images on such warnings every two to three years to increase their effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I would add on this point, finally, that in the dispute on plain packaging against Australia at WTO that I mentioned earlier, the panel concluded, and I quote, that "there is some econometric evidence suggesting that standardised packaging, together with the enlarged GHWs implemented at the same time contributed to the reduction in overall smoking prevalence as well as in cigar smoking prevalence observed after their entry into force." So, it is a point that we have also leaned on and taken notice of in arriving at our measures.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu asked whether the SP Proposal would lead to "down-trading" and an increase in counterfeit tobacco products.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Down-trading describes a phenomenon in which there is a shift from more expensive tobacco products or brands to lower-priced alternatives in the market.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The tobacco industry has contended that standardised packaging will result in this phenomenon, which will, in turn, lead to an increase in overall tobacco demand or consumption because consumers buy more products when prices are lower.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have looked at this with advice from our experts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This shift towards lower-priced tobacco products in the Australian market was observed even before the introduction of standardised packaging, and is also observed in all other high-income countries, not just in Australia, as smoking prevalence decreases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Much of this is attributable to pricing strategies of the tobacco industry itself, which has been known to increase the price differential between low and higher-priced brands when passing on tax increases to the customer.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Our own assessment is that any acceleration in trends towards down-trading in Australia is likely to be largely attributable to the actions of the tobacco industry in differentially passing on the increases in taxes in the years following the implementation of standardised packaging.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Correspondingly, the contribution of standardised packaging to down-trading is likely to only be a modest one, if at all.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Any impact that down-trading may have on increasing overall demand may also be addressed by policy measures to increase the absolute price and, hence, reduce affordability of low-price brands, for example, by increasing tobacco taxes, if necessary.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Regarding counterfeit tobacco products, our assessment is that the introduction of standardised packaging is unlikely to materially contribute towards an increase in illicit trade in tobacco products in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We arrived at this view after having carefully considered the arguments and evidence submitted by the tobacco industry players themselves on illicit trade to the public consultation, as well as, of course, the experience in Australia.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Much of the evidence submitted was in relation to Australia's experience, largely because they have had several years since they introduced the measures, have gathered a large amount of data, and also looked at the experience, in some way, with the benefit of hindsight.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The same evidence was submitted to the WTO Panel, which reviewed it in detail.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The prevailing form of illicit tobacco in Singapore is that of contraband, which is genuine but duty-unpaid cigarettes, as opposed to counterfeit cigarettes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Due to the relatively small Singapore market for cigarettes, counterfeit cigarette manufacturers are not incentivised to counterfeit cigarettes for sale in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In Singapore, illicit tobacco products are sold on the black market rather than at licensed tobacco retailers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The aim of counterfeiting is to "pass off" counterfeit products as the genuine article.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There has been no evidence submitted in the consultations to MOH to show that buyers on the black market will choose counterfeit products in standardised packaging over contraband, genuine products, and that really is the assessment that one has to make.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah has asked whether MOH will be reaching out to retailers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think her concern, quite rightly, was with the retailers who may have an existing stock of the older non-standardised packaging tobacco products and she asked if we could reach out to them, to help them understand the new standardised packaging requirements, hear their feedback, and also to understand any concerns they might have on the implementation deadlines and operationalising of the implementation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: She also asked about the length of the transition period.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These are all very pertinent issues to mitigate any harsh effects there might be against the retailers, particularly those who operate smaller setups.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As mentioned earlier, should this Bill be passed, MOH will brief stakeholders within the industry on the proposed specifications for the standardised layouts for tobacco product packaging so the rules and requirements will be made clear.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In addition, we will also discuss other operational implementation issues that they might have.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Tobacco retailers will be invited to these briefings as well.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As for the transition period that Er Dr Lee Bee Wah raised, other countries that have introduced standardised packaging typically give the industry three months to a year from the publication of the requirements for standardised packaging to the start of the sell-through period that I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will provide something similar for the SP Proposal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On enforcement, Mr Louis Ng asked about this question and suggested that MOH consider setting up a separate institutionalised body to enforce our standardised packaging measure, similar to Australia's Tobacco Plain Packaging Enforcement Committee.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The enforcement of Singapore's tobacco control law already falls under a specialised regulatory agency, namely, HSA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The HSA enforces the labelling requirements for tobacco products, including the existing GHWs, the health information, as well as the sale restriction messages on tobacco packaging.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is usually done at the importer, manufacturer and also the distributor level.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Thus far, we have found the existing regulatory regime to be adequate and sufficient, but we will no doubt keep in mind Mr Louis Ng's suggestion as we consider the details of implementation, if this Bill is passed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Prof Lim Sun Sun raised some very valid points on what happens with the proliferation of social media.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These are all issues that we have to grapple with, not just in tobacco control, but, overall, in terms of the messaging and the type of information that one gleans and gathers on social media, which is very much and very quickly proliferating.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The first is that under our current Tobacco Control of Advertisements and Sales Act, tobacco-related advertisements in all forms of media are already banned and that can include advertisements which emanate from foreign countries overseas but which are viewed or shown in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We prohibit it but, obviously, with so many different influencers and the examples that Prof Lim herself cited where one can artistically and somewhat perhaps very carefully design the way in which the images are portrayed, this makes detection and, therefore, enforcement a lot more difficult.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Nonetheless, we will take on board the suggestion to work more closely with social media companies and the tech giants to ensure that this same message is passed through, which leads to my next point.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: HPB already runs a very extensive public education campaign.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is also done online and that is also done using social media.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, apart from enforcing it through the rules which we have in place, we also want to amplify our public education outreach on the same platforms with the same reach and, hopefully, to the same target audience as what these tobacco companies are trying to do.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will continue to do so and see how we can take on board Prof Lim Sun Sun's suggestions as to how we can work more closely with these companies, particularly on the point about algorithms, which is entirely valid.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng has asked us to clarify the rationale behind the increase in maximum fines for offences under section 18 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As mentioned earlier, the aim is to align the maximum penalties in section 18 with the maximum fines for similarly serious comparable offences pertaining to the importation, distribution, retail and possession of prohibited tobacco products and imitation tobacco products under sections 15 and 16 of the Bill, respectively.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: With the alignment of penalties, we make it clear that offences related to unlicensed dealing of tobacco products are considered as serious offences to the same degree as offences relating to prohibited tobacco products.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked if we have the profile of smokers in each age group.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Based on our population health surveys, we do have information on the general demographic profile of smokers by age group and that is in part why we are concerned with the initiation of smokers, especially at a young age.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: HPB uses such information to customise and also target the education programmes and smoking cessation interventions for specific demographic groups in settings, such as schools, workplaces, healthcare and also in the community.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For instance, HPB has developed the Ramadan I Quit smoking cessation programme to meet the specific needs of the community.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Roadshows are held in various festive bazaars annually to provide cessation support to smokers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, it is not just the campaign on the awareness but also providing these smokers who are keen to stop with our support for the cessation programme.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In 2018, over 4,000 participants from all ethnic groups pledged to quit smoking.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: HPB has worked closely with the Ministry of Education as well as with Institutes of Higher Learning to increase education and awareness to prevent youths from taking up tobacco products or, for those who have started, to stop.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: HPB is further leveraging social media to better engage youths on the benefits of a smoke-free lifestyle, and to persuade the young to stay smoke-free.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah has urged the Government again to consider DSPs in more places, especially in residential areas.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This does not quite concern standardised packaging, but nonetheless, I understand that my colleagues at the Ministry of the Environment and Water Resources are monitoring the effectiveness of the Orchard Road No-Smoking Zone before considering whether to replicate the concept elsewhere, perhaps in the estates that Er Dr Lee Bee Wah mentioned.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will ask them to consider Er Dr Lee Bee Wah's suggestion to study the effectiveness of the DSPs in other areas, and the feasibility of piloting a similar No-Smoking Zone concept in residential estates.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah also asked what we are doing to tackle cigarette smuggling.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Singapore Customs' enforcement teams already, as Members know, conduct operations to interdict supply and distribution of duty-unpaid cigarettes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Customs works closely with other law enforcement agencies, such as the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority and the Singapore Police Force, to interdict cigarette smuggling into Singapore and also enforce against illegal street peddlers and end-consumers to suppress street-level duty-unpaid cigarette activities.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Customs also organises targeted outreach programmes and community road shows.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Of course, finally, members of the public can report illegal activities to the Singapore Customs through a 24-hour hotline, by email or on the mobile app Customs@SG.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah also suggested that penalties for unlicensed import of tobacco products under the Tobacco Act can include a jail term under the Tobacco Act itself.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Currently, selling or dealing in duty-unpaid tobacco are already serious offences under the Customs Act.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The penalties are severe and they are designed to deter those who may be thinking of engaging in such activities.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong asked two questions related to this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The first is, whether or not, once our standardised packaging measure is in place, one could still import non-compliant cigarette packs into Singapore simply by paying the duty.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, whether duty is paid or unpaid, the fact of the matter is that if the packaging for the purposes of importation into Singapore does not comply with the regulations, then that would not be allowed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
